name: Hair fibres (Toppik)

card.summary: Keratin-style cosmetic fibres that cling to existing hair to disguise thinning; a cover-up rather than a treatment, with a rare eye-injury case report.
card.aka: Toppik, hair building fibers, reconstructive hair fibers
card.note: A case report describes a fibre entering the eye and causing uveitis.

quick.overview:
Hair fibres such as Toppik are fine powders that bind to existing hair by static electricity to make thinning areas look fuller. They disguise hair loss rather than treating it.

Published research is limited to a 2017 microscopy analysis of five brands and a 2020 case report of eye injury.
quick.mechanism: Electrostatically charged fibres adhere to the hair shaft, thickening its appearance and reducing visible scalp. Effects last until washed out.
quick.risks: A 2020 case report described anterior uveitis after a fibre from a hair-building product entered the eye of a 73-year-old man.

lead: Hair fibres, sold under brands such as Toppik, are cosmetic powders made of tiny fibres that cling to existing hair and make thinning areas look fuller. They are used by men and women to disguise hair loss at the crown, part line, temples or hairline, giving the look of denser hair within minutes and without surgery or medication.[1][4]

A 2017 study in the International Journal of Trichology describes these products as reconstructive hair fibres, an electrostatic adherent powder that bonds to the hair shaft and can disguise hair loss. It used scanning electron microscopy and X-ray microanalysis to compare the shape, structure and chemical composition of five brands, among them Toppik, which it reports is made of animal keratin from sheep's wool.[1][5]

Hair fibres sit among the concealment options for hair loss, alongside comb-overs, hats, wigs and toupees, while medications and transplants are separate treatment routes.[2] They change how hair looks rather than how it grows. Toppik's own page describes the fibres as keratin nearly identical to human hair, sold in nine shades and used for the hairline, part, crown, roots and beard.[4]

angle.text: Fibres thicken the apparent diameter of existing hair, so thin patches show less scalp. The effect is temporary and visible immediately, which is why users apply them before events or daily as part of styling.

paras: Reconstructive hair fibres are described as organic fibres of fine powder that carry an electrostatic charge so they adhere to the existing hair shaft. A laboratory analysis of five brands examined their shape, morphology and chemical composition.[1][5] The fibres do not grow hair or affect the follicle.

Toppik's page says its fibres cling to existing hair and stay in place through rain, wind and sweat until the next wash; the company sells a spray called FiberHold intended to strengthen the bond between fibres and hair, plus a coloured hair thickener and a hairline filler.[4] These are manufacturer statements.

The 2017 study found that products differ in what they are made of. One brand was cotton-based cellulose; one was plant-derived keratin from corn, soybean, fig and linseed; a third combined cotton fibres with a smooth second fibre type; Toppik was described as animal keratin from sheep's wool; and Nanogen as pure, positively charged keratin.[5]

Under the electron microscope, the cotton and plant products showed fibres lying in parallel arrangements, while the Toppik and Nanogen samples showed scaly microfibres whose cuticle pattern closely resembled natural hair.[5] X-ray microanalysis found high sulfur, carbon and oxygen in these two keratin products, consistent with keratin, and mainly carbon and oxygen in the cotton one.[5]

People use fibres to make a thinning crown, widening part or receding temples look denser for a photo, an event or daily routine. Toppik lists the beard, hairline, thinning spots and roots as areas of use and suggests mixing shades for a closer colour match.[4] Because the fibres bind to existing strands, they depend on some hair being present.[5]

Wikipedia's hair loss article lists comb-overs, hats and wigs or toupees as concealment approaches, noting that wigs vary widely in quality and cost, and places minoxidil, finasteride, dutasteride and hair transplantation in the separate group of treatments for loss itself.[2] Fibres are commonly discussed as a short-term bridge or companion to those routes, and the article text does not itself name hair fibres.[2]

The 2017 authors report that, despite the chemical differences, the five products gave similar cosmetic results in the patients tested, and that fibres worked well for most types of hair loss but did not stick to bald patches in alopecia areata, which they attribute to reliance on static electricity to bond with existing hair. They describe the study as small and as assessing only immediate appearance.[5]

No studies found of long-term clinical outcomes. A laboratory study analysed the shape, structure and chemical composition of five brands of reconstructive hair fibres and assessed immediate cosmetic appearance in a small group of patients.[1][5]

The reported harm is a single case report from 2020 of a 73-year-old man with his first episode of acute anterior uveitis, in whom a white fibre was found penetrating the cornea into the anterior chamber; he identified it as coming from a cosmetic hair-building product. The authors discussed earlier literature on small foreign fibres causing eye disease.[3]

timeline.event: A laboratory study compares five brands of reconstructive hair fibres by electron microscopy and X-ray microanalysis.[1][5]
A case report describes uveitis linked to a fibre from a hair enhancement product.[3]

lore.intro: Product claims for hair fibres are made mainly by manufacturers, and the published research on them is small.[4][5]

claims.claim: Fibres stay on through rain, wind and sweat until the next wash
claims.believers: Toppik's page says the keratin fibres cling to existing hair and hold through weather and sweat; a hold spray is sold to strengthen the bond.[4]
claims.experts: The 2017 study describes the bond as electrostatic and assessed only immediate appearance; no published trial tested durability under different conditions.[5]

claims.claim: Fibres work on any thinning area
claims.believers: The manufacturer lists hairline, crown, beard and roots as areas of use.[4]
claims.experts: The 2017 authors report the fibres did not adhere to bald patches in alopecia areata, because they rely on static attraction to existing hair.[5]

claims.believers: They are sold as a cosmetic that is applied and washed out.[4]
claims.experts: A 2020 case report links a fibre from a hair-building product to anterior uveitis in one man.[3]
